Includes living room, bedrooms, kitchen, and toilets.1,000 INR 6,500 Built-up Area Carpet Area PLUS the area of inner and outer walls, and private balconies/terraces.1,150 INR 5,652 Super Built-up Area Built-up Area PLUS a proportional share of common areas (lifts, lobby, stairs, club house). (Assuming a 30% Loading Factor)1,300 INR 5,000 In this case, a buyer is paying INR 65,00,000 for a unit advertised at INR 5,000 per sq. ft. - based on Super Built-up Area. [...] Whereas, in reality, the space that is usable by a buyer, the actual area on which to lay carpets or live, is only 1,000 sq. ft. This means the true cost for the net usable space (Carpet Area) is INR 6,500 per square foot. The loading factor is 30% and represents the additional 300 sq. ft. that the buyer pays for to compensate for common amenities. This calculation shows why there is a need to always negotiate the price of the property on the Carpet Area as specified by RERA. ## What does a super built-up area include Built-up area of the flat Clubhouses Air Ducts Pipe/Shaft ducts Lifts Staircases Lobby Swimming pool Gymnasium Other Common Facilities ## Loading Factor [...] Before RERA require home builders to sell homes by carpeted square footage, built square footage was widely used as a unit of space to take advantage of the ambiguity in space calculations. Using skyscraper square footage as a unit of measure helped lower the cost per square foot of real estate. It also gave buyers the false impression that they were investing in a large house when they really weren’t. Suppose a 1,000-square-foot carpeted house costs 2,000 rupees per square foot. In such a scenario, the total cost of the property is Rs. 20,000,000. To make the marketing pitch even more attractive, the developer will offer a super built-up area (say 1,300 sq ft) and slash the property price at Rs 1,800 per sq ft.
